input: Label all the breaker switches in the fuse box

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: There may be one or multiple fuse boxes/panels in the home — knowing how many and where they are changes the scale of the task entirely.
Whether breakers are currently unlabeled, partially labeled, or mislabeled determines how much discovery/testing work is needed before any labeling can happen.
Knowing if this is a solo job or involves a helper matters because safely mapping circuits (flipping breakers and checking which outlets/lights go out) is much easier and safer with two people.
Access to tools like a circuit tracer or outlet tester vs. relying on manual trial-and-error significantly affects how accurately and quickly breakers can be identified.
The physical label format — handwritten tape, printed labels, an official panel directory card — affects what materials are needed and the final quality of the result.
The naming convention used (e.g., room-based like 'Kitchen Outlets', circuit-based, or appliance-specific) determines how detailed and useful the labels will be to others in the household.
Understanding whether 'done' means every single breaker is verified and labeled vs. just the unknown ones are filled in sets the bar for how thorough the process needs to be.

gold.taskTitle: Label all breaker switches in the fuse box
gold.taskDescription: Identify and label every breaker switch in the fuse box so each one is clearly matched to the circuit or area it controls.

questions.title: How many fuse boxes or panels does your home have?
questions.description: Determine the number and locations of all electrical panels that need to be labeled.

questions.title: Are the breakers currently unlabeled, partial, or mislabeled?
questions.description: Understand the current state of the panel to estimate how much circuit-discovery work is needed before labeling.

questions.title: Will someone be helping you, or is this a solo job?
questions.description: Assess whether a second person is available to check outlets/lights while breakers are flipped, which is the safest and most efficient approach.

questions.title: Do you have a circuit tracer, outlet tester, or just basic tools?
questions.description: Identify what equipment is on hand to map each breaker to its circuit accurately.

questions.title: What format do you want the labels to be in?
questions.description: Decide on the physical labeling method — handwritten tape, a label maker, printed inserts — to know what materials to gather.

questions.title: How detailed should each label's description be?
questions.description: Establish the naming convention, such as room-level (e.g., 'Master Bedroom'), appliance-specific (e.g., 'Refrigerator'), or circuit-code style.

questions.title: Does every breaker need verifying, or just the unknown ones?
questions.description: Define what 'fully done' looks like — whether all breakers must be tested and confirmed or only the currently blank/unclear ones need attention.
